en: Preface:
Since Fuxi drew the trigrams and Cangjie created writing, the world first opened with characters. Once characters were established, the Three Teachings subsequently emerged;
these three teachings are the progenitors of written texts, all originating from a single source. This being so, when we come to...

Later, the Three Teachings diverged and each became the written record of its own school. Yet, if one examines the intent behind their foundational statements, they all ultimately converge upon the exhaustion of nature and the attainment of destiny (*xingming*).
They employ these means to awaken the minds of people and clarify their innate awareness, expounding the source of the Great Way to provide instruction for the world;
fundamentally, there was no difference between them. However, as heterodox views arose in profusion, those who sought to align themselves with these teachings each established their own sects.

Households [are divided], with each side taking up defensive positions and mutually denouncing the other as wrong. Thus, the texts of the Three Teachings, which were originally intended to rectify the world, instead cause the world to be disturbed by them.
This is not something that causes only the Tathāgata to frown; even Confucius and Laozi would knit their brows at it.
The doctrine of the solitary life-force cannot be divided; thus, while the texts of the Three Teachings often differ in their wording, they establish their doctrines as being identical.
This *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* directly aligns with Confucius and Mencus and surpasses Laozi.
This is because the primary purport of this scripture’s meaning takes enlightened nature (*bodhicitta*) as its essential aim, seeking to penetrate all things through that enlightened nature.

This treatise appears shallow yet is profound; it seems empty yet is substantial. Its doctrine originates from the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*), accords with the inherent goodness of human nature (*xing shan*), and clarifies the Way (*dao*) and its Virtue (*de*).

Because it consists of only fifty words, it is able to awaken and enlighten everyone from the highest sages to the most ignorant, enabling them to clarify the mind and realize their true nature (*xinxing*).
This is why this scripture serves as the progenitor of all other scriptures. However, within it, the six sense-objects (*liuchen*)...
Regarding the discourse on the four marks of merit and the giving of alms, the questions and answers from beginning to end do not go beyond this:
the general vision of the causal nature of awakening. Because it does not arise from subsequent conditioning, it is used to dispel the delusions of people and lead them into the Way.
As for its most essential function, it does not lie outside the single word "subduing" (*damana*). Its reversal of what is natural is particularly emphasized; there is nothing else.

Abiding and arising, his mind is focused on a single word. Therefore, those who preach this sutra must not misrepresent the true purport of our Tathāgata with discourses on emptiness and quiescent extinction.

On the full moon of the second month in the year of Xinchou, the practitioner Daoren visited Mount Kuanglu, while the lay-devotee Zizhen was also traveling through Jiangyou; they encountered me at Zhulin Monastery and conversed together.
Regarding worldly affairs, there is no further meaning to be found. Yet you, Zhenli, truly desire to conceive the thought of saving others amidst the mundane world.
Consequently, the Daoist went with him to Mount Wei; Mount Wei was a place where Zhenli had previously traveled.

The terrain was surrounded by mountains and encircled by water, making it a truly suitable place for seclusion. The Daoist was pleased and remained there. Among them were two or three disciples who were quite...
"Excellent diligence! My son, you truly have a karmic affinity with me from former lives. You have thus requested that I explain the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At first, I hesitated; however, I subsequently saw that you possess sincerity sufficient to carry this matter through from beginning to end."
Having requested this from the Tathāgata, he received his compassionate instructions and established a ritual altar for a lecture series, which was completed in forty days.

The disciples further requested that the Master compose a preface for it. The Master then reflected that while there were dozens or even hundreds of commentaries on this sutra, most belonged to the genre of Chan school records and Buddhist "public cases" (gong'an), failing to capture the essential meaning of the Tathāgata’s exposition of the sutra. Therefore—
I have specifically taken the words and meanings within this scripture to examine the meaning through the words,

bringing them all back to perfect enlightenment so that neither those who see nor those who hear shall harbor even the slightest doubt or deficiency. Although there may be slight differences from the treatises of other Buddhist schools,
in opening the true countenance of the Tathāgata and revealing the Tathāgata’s true and wondrous truth, it does not go beyond such knowing and such seeing.
This view is merely a matter of faith and understanding. To summarize, the True Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) taught in the Buddha’s doctrine originates from the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
There has never been a case where the principle is not real while one speaks of emptiness in a superficial or vague manner.

Indeed, the Tathāgata’s teaching on True Emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*) is fundamentally based on the fact that the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*) is inherently non-existent, void, and spirit-like, such that no signs can be grasped. Yet later interpreters have abandoned this primary intent.
I have selected its coarse traces: throughout all the sutras, matters such as the six sense-objects, the four marks, merit, and giving are elaborated into chapters;
yet these are like a fool speaking in a dream—what benefit do they have for the awakened nature?

This is why the understanding of the Way-man places singular importance on the single phrase "samyak-saṃbodhi. For this phrase is truly the governing principle of a single sutra, and it unifies the three teachings.

Regarding the source and flow [of these teachings]: if one grasps their essential intent, then the doctrines of the various sutras and the Way of the Three Teachings will be unified and thoroughly integrated.

From the outset, there has never been anything obscure, mysterious, or difficult to believe that could serve as an excuse for later generations. Yet ordinary people harbor many doubts even regarding oral instructions received directly from the lips of a master;
how much more so can they be relied upon when based on the words of a spirit medium? Therefore, one should simply refrain from engaging in such practices.
The discourse produced here is free of affectations and flowery rhetoric; it contains only the principles of exhausting one's nature and fulfilling one's destiny.

It is clear and lucid, so that we may hope not to incur the reproach of the Tathāgata, and furthermore, enable those who follow the teachings of Confucius and Laozi to see that the words of the Daoist masters (daoren) are not deceptive talk for deceiving the world.
Hereafter, should there be any authors who can edit and disseminate these according to the intent of the Daoist masters—this [is my hope].
This commentary may also serve as a mirror for all within the realm.
Written by the Daoist Yunfeng from the spirit tablet on the fifth day before the full moon of the fourth month in the year of Xinchou.

In discussing the relationship between the lady and the immortal, though they were separated by their physical forms, they were united through their spirits. That which they achieved through this union was not accidental;
there must have been a cause for their meeting. Thus, they were able to come together and achieve success. I have often deliberated upon this.
The traces of the immortals in this world are as if both present and absent. They are like the wind that possesses sound;
when it encounters objects, it produces resonance. One cannot grasp the sound and take it to be the wind, yet one cannot say that the sound is not the wind.
However, to claim there is sound without form would be considered nearly preposterous; thus, all words from spirit-writing (ji-shu) involve the ethereal and are difficult to verify.

Therefore, both King Mu of Zhou and Emperor Wu of Han were fond of the arts of the immortals; they began by believing, yet subsequently grew suspicious, until finally they completely repudiated everything they had done throughout their lives.
Thus, it is clearly evident from the classics and historical records that the claims of the immortals are not to be relied upon.
How could I dare to entrust myself to the realm of the immortals and rely on a spirit medium to delude the world? Nevertheless, I...
There is a point to be made here. To rely on the words of a single spirit medium is unreliable; when such a person recounts matters that cannot be verified, it is an illusion.

Yet, if there were sacred scriptures within this world that a divine immortal could read, and if that immortal could explain the profound meanings contained within those scriptures—would this be an illusion, or would it not be an illusion? Regarding this, I do not presume to judge for myself.
Regarding the immortals, he was fond of making words that could not be verified.

However, as for his compilation of the *Tathāgata-vajra-sūtra* into a single volume, he did so not merely for the sake of his disciples, but directly to resolve the doubts of all people in future generations and to provide a common basis for realizing this interpretation. Indeed, I obtained this interpretation from Master Yunfeng, and Yun...
Master Feng further obtained this in the land of India, receiving the teachings of the Tathāgata directly;
it was only then that he was able to transmit it through spirit-writing (*jishu*). How could I possibly have achieved the merit of "investigation and understanding"?

Yet, I cannot help but humbly attach myself to the end of those who possess such investigation and understanding, for there are truly three difficulties regarding the method of investigation and understanding. The first difficulty lies in the directness of the understanding.
Yet, it has not yet attained profundity. Second, the difficulty lies in the brevity of the language, which has not yet achieved detailed exposition.
Third, the difficulty lies in discarding all the *yulu* (recorded sayings) and *gongan* (public cases) of the Chan school, while failing to move the ears and eyes of the common world.
To provide an illustration using essential points from the sutras: consider names such as Jetavana, the Ganges, and Mount Sumeru.
The old editions all contained illustrations and precise indications of distances in *li*, yet these have now been entirely excised.

For instance, the names and origins of figures such as the asura Kāliṅga and the Cakravartin kings, which were previously recorded, have likewise been deleted. This is also the case with the term *sambodhi*.

Thus, following the traditional interpretation, the term "samādhi of correct awakening" (zhèngjué sānmèi) takes the character *mèi* (obscuration/insentience) directly as a counterpart to the character *jué* (awakening).

Regarding the four fruits of the bodhisattva, the traditional interpretation held that terms such as *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) and so forth were merely appellations; now, they are instead interpreted as "entering the stream" and "returning once more."
Nirvana is interpreted as "the other shore," and the Buddha-field as "the superior land"; both differ from alternative interpretations.

Regarding "prior lives" and "the past," as well as "future" and "present," they were previously understood as "former existences" and "this life. Now, the meanings of these characters have been clearly illuminated.
As for various names and forms that may be transmitted but cannot be fully verified, there are none in which the redundant has not been excised for the sake of concision.
In some cases, the scriptural text contains but a single word, yet the analytical interpretation must be exhaustive;
in other cases, the scriptural text contains a succession of words, yet they are summarized with broad strokes. These are all the essential points of this scripture.
Thus, while Master Yunfeng alone spoke clearly and intelligibly regarding those parts not yet fully understood by the world, my opportunity to participate in the study of this scripture—its...
Not even two or three parts of it have been translated. Nevertheless, I have something further to say:

that this scripture was able to receive its commentary was due to the good fortune of meeting the Great Master at Mount Kuang-lu, and likewise the good fortune of meeting his various disciples in the new settlement, whereby we were able to join together in accomplishing this work.
The arrival of Master Yunfeng was originally brought about by the steadfast sincerity of his disciples.
However, speaking of my own relationship with these disciples, they were all born in Yunjian and have resided in Jiangyou;

they share a long-standing karmic affinity with me from previous lives, and having now met again in this land, I have thus made this vow to welcome the Great Master to the new settlement to open the altar and establish the teachings.

The lectures were completed after forty days. They began on the nineteenth day of the second month of the *xinchou* year and concluded on the ninth day of the fourth month. Throughout these forty days, the Great Master and his disciples—
Although the realms of the immortals and the mundane are separated, their spiritual essence naturally communicates. Thus, we were unaware of how swiftly this was accomplished;
both I and my disciples have all attained realization of the Tathāgata’s sublime purport and have been permitted to follow in the Great Master’s footsteps to transmit his name.
It is not that the disciples have failed to contribute to this end. Alas! The celestial and the human are not distant; how could the immortal and the mundane be so far apart?
If one can maintain the nature of awakening within oneself, it will be fitting for this day.
Thus, that the book obtained today was channeled through the spirit-writing board (*jī*) and published for the world is not without its cause.

May all disciples exhort one another to uphold and explain it, so that those in future generations throughout the world shall not regard the way of the immortals as mere fabrication or delusion. Furthermore—
May we together behold the true countenance of the Tathāgata.
On the day after the full moon in the fourth month of the early summer of the year Xinchou, Gu Zimen Zhen recorded this via spirit-writing at his ancestral home in Weishan.
*The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Spirit-writing by Grand Master Yunfeng;
revised by Shi Guzong Zi Zhen.
Chapter One: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, at the hour of eating, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered [the city].
He went for alms in the great city of Śrāvastī. Having finished his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location.
When he had finished his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.
The Sublime Discourse on the Single Sūtra of the Vajra was spoken by the Tathāgata. Its essential purport is that true emptiness is signless;
it begins with the words "Thus have I heard" and concludes with the teaching of "Suchness, immovable. Thus, its beginning and end are in perfect correspondence.
Yunfeng said: "If it is thus, it is so; if not thus, it is not so. If it is 'thus-ness' (ruru), there is nothing at all that is 'so.
One must not speak entirely as if giving a formal lecture. If it is thus, I have obtained and heard it;
if it is not thus, then even if there is preaching of the Dharma, it cannot be considered heard by me. Regarding the phrase "At one time the Buddha was... this refers to seeing the Buddha.
At this time, if one desires to hear the Dharma but does not see the Buddha present, it is because one's resolve is not yet firm.

Now that the Buddha is already here and what I am hearing is being spoken, is it not most certain? These two sentences show that the compiler intends to demonstrate that what was heard and witnessed was the Tathāgata manifesting his body to preach the Dharma.
Zi Zhen’s Account: Śrāvastī is located to the east of India in the Western Regions. At that time, the Buddha happened to visit this country, though it was not his permanent residence.
The Jeta Grove (Jetavana) is named after Prince Jeta, who planted the trees there; this is a literary description of the scene.
As for the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden, it is the place where Anāthapiṇḍika formerly provided alms to the destitute and solitary.
At that time, the Buddha was in that garden, dwelling together with a community of bhikṣus. "Bhikṣu" is a term for a disciple.
A bhikṣu is called "great" because he has mastered the principles of the Way, much like a disciple at a high seat.
At that time, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty people living together there.
Yunfeng said: This passage states that the Buddha was in this place and that those who followed him were numerous;
seeing his faith, they followed him. To be with him, one must necessarily hear from him. These three phrases describe the manner in which the Buddha was able to transform his disciples.
The Discourse on the True Son: At that time, the World-Honored One—there is no "World-Honored One" other than the Buddha.
By virtue of the title bestowed upon a sage, the Buddha is the most honored among men; thus, the Buddha is called the World-Honored One, yet it refers to one and the same Buddha.
He was wearing robes and a *kaṣāya* (a shoulder-cloth). Some say these are garments of gentleness. He held an almsbowl, which is the bowl of the dragon Upananda; some say [it is so].
The bowl offered by the Heavenly King was brought into this city of Śrāvastī for the purpose of begging for alms.
Before the Dharma was preached, he first engaged in begging for alms to stir the perceptions and hearing of the multitude.

Having completed his sequential rounds of begging, it was like a painting of non-abiding; there was no need to discuss whether the amount received was much or little, for once the begging was finished, all was done.
Without leaving behind even a hair’s breadth of unextinguished thought, he returned to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Within the state of non-abiding, there is nevertheless a place of abiding; thus it is called the "Root.
Having finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, thereby completing one cycle of the alms-round. After washing his feet—not merely for the sake of physical cleanliness—he purified his mind.
Yunfeng said: The three phrases regarding the completion of the meal may be explained as a single sequence. Zizhen said:
As for the one who spreads the seats, he alone sets up a high seat above the twelve hundred and fifty disciples;
at this time, they have already sat down, and the World-Honored One is about to preach the Dharma.
Yunfeng said: "The mere completion of begging for food and the mere passing of time washing one's feet are both places where the Buddha attained his mind.
Therefore, he spread out his seat and remained entirely free from attachment. When people sit in stillness for even a single moment, myriad conditions arise;
it is not that they are insufficient, but rather that they seek something more, and thus they spring up in agitation. The World-Honored One has already [transcended] this."
Forgetting the matter of begging for food is the root source from which the mark of non-self (anātman-lakṣaṇa) unfolds.

○ In the second section, "The Chapter on Subhūti’s Request," when the Elder Subhūti was among the great assembly, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and placed his right knee [on the ground].
They descended to the ground, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; the Tathāgata well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One, how should sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi abide? How should they subdue their minds? The Buddha said, "Excellent."
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas.

Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you: how a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide and how they should subdue their minds. Only.
"Nevertheless, World-Honored One, I wish and desire to hear the true teaching of the son.
Among the elder disciples numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty, there was one of great virtue;
Subhūti had three names: the first was Kūṇika (Born of Emptiness), the second was Bhadrika (Well-Appeared), and the third was Subhūti."
This refers to the title he received upon attaining the fruit of realization. Regarding his rising from his seat amidst the great assembly:
at that time, although the World-Honored One had already spread out his seat and the great assembly were all seated, Subhūti alone rose from among the seats.
At that moment, as for the garment he wore, he bared one shoulder—specifically the right shoulder—which is the custom of the clothing in the Western Regions.
The preparation was in this manner for all. It was not that Subhūti alone wore these robes. "Placing the right knee on the ground" refers to the present-day practice of kneeling.
The reason only "right" is mentioned and not "left" is a convention of abbreviation in written language.
To say "with palms joined in reverence" and address the Buddha is merely to respectfully seek the World-Honored One’s intention to preach the Dharma; it is truly rare.
These two characters are spoken by Subhūti as words of praise: "The World-Honored One (Bhagavān) is a rare being in this world, and is uniquely honored among all in the world. Yunfeng said:
"Tathāgata is precisely the Buddha; he is precisely the World-Honored One. Regarding these two characters, 'Tathāgata,' there are two [meanings]."
Regarding its meaning: if spoken of in terms of stillness, it is like still water; if spoken of in terms of responsiveness, it is like flowing spring water.
When it is still, myriad stimuli do not move it; when it flows, a hundred thoughts do not obstruct it.
Therefore, it is called "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One). These two characters, "Tathāgata," possess profound significance. According to ancient exegesis, it is "tranquil and unmoving," yet responsive...
And thus it is thoroughly penetrated. This merely refers to the meaning of the word "Tathāgata. Now, that which comes must necessarily come from somewhere;
yet, in being exactly as it comes, its coming does not rely upon the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). As for these characteristics of dharmas...
Regarding what occurs after [the present] and before the future, there is no dharma-characteristic; there is only *tathatā* (suchness).
For suchness is the source of the awakened nature (*bodhata*). Thus, when that source has not yet emerged, suchness is contained within the nature;
when it has already emerged, suchness is realized within the mind. This is why the character "like" (*ru*) cannot be understood as a mere void. Suchness.
As for "coming": if it were according to suchness, it would not be "coming. That which is suchness cannot come; that which comes has not yet reached suchness, nor can it suddenly arrive.
To speak of them as a whole, where is there that is not suchness? Where is there that is not arriving at suchness?
Its coming from suchness to this place further advances beyond the two lines [of the verse] concerning "tranquil and unmoving."

The previous explanation was close to being merely illustrative; now, I shall again explain it according to the literal meaning of the original text. Taken as a whole, it is unified by the character "ru" (thus/as).
When explained in terms of reaching the nature of awakening, there is nothing that is not thus.
The True Discourse on the Sons: "He skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas. These bodhisattvas are the twelve hundred and fifty people.
"Bodhisattva" is a general term. "Skillfully protects" means that the Tathāgata is able to protect all bodhisattvas with wholesome mindfulness (*smṛti*).
"Mindfulness" refers specifically to the Tathāgata’s mindfulness. "Skillfully entrusts" corresponds to the preceding phrase; the meaning is as follows:
If he comes to be able to protect and keep in mind all bodhisattvas, then he will certainly be able to entrust this Dharma to them and commit it to their care.
This section represents Subhūti’s aspiration; it is the opening statement regarding the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma.
Regarding the "Words of Zizhen": The two characters "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*) here are Subhūti calling upon the Buddha’s name to request the preaching of the Dharma.
Generally, whenever the title "World-Honored One" appears later in the text, it refers to Subhūti addressing the Tathāgata with honor.
As for the men and women mentioned as being outside the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty people, they are men and women who possess virtuous thoughts.
People have gathered here together to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Yunfeng said: "To 'give rise' (*fa*) is like the dharma of generation. The character *a* is a particle.
The three characters *nuttara* are translated as the two characters 'unsurpassed' (*wúshàng*). The two characters *samyak* are translated as the two characters 'correctly equal' (*zhèngděng*)."
Regarding the explanation of the term *tri-bodhi*: it is translated as the two characters "correct awakening" (*zhèngjué*).

This is because although human beings possess this mind, if they are submerged in sensual desires, it cannot manifest. It is like a sprout that has just begun to grow when it is obscured by other things.
Thus, one desires to sprout but cannot sprout. Therefore, the word "emerges" (fa) is employed; "emerges" means to follow that which is born. What is meant by "unsurpassed"?
It means there is not a single thing that can further be added above it. As for "perfectly equal":
It is said that this unsurpassed mind is equal in every respect, from the Tathāgatas and the various bodhisattvas down to all sentient beings;
all alike attain this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. As for "perfect enlightenment," it means that this mind is neither biased nor partial.

It is like the sun suspended in the center of the sky, casting shadows that are square and upright; it shines everywhere throughout the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, leaving nothing unawakened.
This is called "Perfect Awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). From this very first point of spiritual light, one remains untainted by worldly desires.

Regardless of whether one belongs to the superior, middling, or inferior of the three vehicles, each and every individual possesses this awakened mind. The character "zheng" (正) is written as "zhèng" (證).

Explanation: The character "zheng" (正) at the bottom is explained as the character "zhong" (中). Taken together, this refers collectively to all bodhisattvas who today listen to the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
they are all able to give rise to this unsurpassable, perfectly upright mind of right awakening (*samyaksambodhi-citta*).
They simply do not yet know how to abide [in it] or how to subdue [the afflictions]. Thus says the Śākya.
This phrase is like the Confucian teaching of "being cautious when alone. To be "alone" means to be without counterpart; this is the supreme commentary.
Whenever there is a matter with a counterpart—such as the categories of before and after—one speaks of the "supreme," which then has no equal.
This fundamental reality has been spoken of since time immemorial; it is like the Confucian doctrine of the inherent goodness of human nature. The Confucians speak of it solely...
The Tathāgata has further taught nine kinds [of beings]. This is the intention to deliver all sentient beings to the end.
Yet, every person possesses this supreme mind of luminous awakening; it is only that they do not know the method by which to cultivate it.
Why is this? It is because as wholesome thoughts arise, unwholesome thoughts follow in their wake; thus, one fails to maintain awareness.
Even if one does become aware of them, one cannot attain the supreme mind. Now I ask the World-Honored One: since these men and women possess wholesome thoughts, how should they abide?
What is meant by "how"? It refers to the manner of intention. As for "should abide," it concerns ordinary people.
When this wholesome thought arises, how can one cause it to remain firm and not depart, so that it dwells constantly within the mind?

Yunfeng further said: "One should not dwell [upon it] by means of forced grasping or fixed concentration, but rather ensure that at the moment the thought arises, it is perceived with perfect clarity; then it will not stray. What does it mean to "subdue the mind"?
This mind is not a separate mind from [the previous one]. Only a wholesome mind can understand it, whereas a defiled mind merely follows along with it.
Therefore, at the moment a defiled mind arises in succession, one must subdue it through the power of great awakening.

To subdue it is like restraining a venomous dragon, subduing a fierce tiger, or warding off a powerful bandit; if one lacks even a little [strength], one will instead be subdued by it. That is to say:
Though it is suppressed, it sprouts again; its intensity becomes even more extreme.

To suppress and subdue it—not by forceful suppression, but because that which abides is the Constant—then that which is subdued will vanish away and undergo silent transformation. These two sentences constitute a single gateway for entering the path to the World-Honored One.
Yunfeng spoke again: "One should view the two phrases, 'should abide thus' and 'should subdue the mind thus,' as a single unit.
It is not that one should abide thus and then separately subdue the mind; rather, one abides in that which is the proper object of abiding."
Thus, that which one ought not to dwell upon will naturally subdue one.
It is simply because people plant their feet where they should not dwell that they experience an additional layer of lack of self-mastery; how then could they remain for long?
When they cannot remain for long and depart again, those things that restrain them all leap forth to seize them.
Regarding the Master Zhen’s explanation of the Buddha’s words, “Excellent, excellent”: this is a praise for the excellence of his inquiry.
Thus, he calls him by name, saying “Subhūti,” which is similar to the Confucian practice of addressing disciples by their given names. The meaning is: “It is just as you have said.
The word “said” (shuō) constitutes the following two phrases. The addition of the two characters “Tathāgata” (Rúlái) serves to demonstrate that [the teaching] is excellent.
To protect and mindfully regard all bodhisattvas, and to entrust them with this teaching, is precisely the Buddha’s fundamental intention;
it is what he brought forth in response to their inquiry. It is also a method for awakening beings by meeting them where they are.
When the World-Honored One speaks of "good sons and good daughters" and so forth, having this supreme and foremost [teaching], it is for them to collectively realize and witness this enlightenment.
With such a mind, one should abide and subdue it in this manner. This is what the Tathāgata has taught regarding the intention:
if a person has a place of abiding yet cannot abide therein, they will be unable to subdue their mind.
Therefore, regarding the place of abiding, there should be neither excess nor deficiency; one must arrive exactly at this state of abiding.
Therefore, the Buddha said, "Abide thus. This is like the Confucian saying, "knowing where to stop. To stop at that which one ought to stop is precisely the gloss for "abiding thus.
People suffer because they do not know how to abide; they simply hand over this mind [to external objects]. How could there be anything to subdue?
The minds of the common and ignorant are sluggish and lack discernment, whereas those of the mediocre person—

The mind begins to move upon contact. As for the minds of sages and worthies, which are still yet capable of penetration, their differentiation and demarcation consist merely in the divergence of the state of abiding.
Why is this? One who is able to abide simply ceases according to that very abiding.
One who cannot abide—if there is a mind of excess, one immediately falls into demonic obstacles; if there is a mind of deficiency, one immediately descends into evil.

yet, upon investigation, the essentials of explaining this sutra are originally not many: they do not exceed [the realization of] emptiness, the characteristics of emptiness, and the non-abiding of dharmas.

"Scattered in their respective places.

This further uses an inverse statement to clarify the principle of the Mahāyāna, the Supreme Vehicle. In every place, wherever this sutra exists, there it is found.

Thus, he simply allowed the burden to remain upon him. Once it had been taken up, however, it could not be cast from the shoulder;

This is for those of the Lesser Vehicle; it opens a dharma-gate for individual renewal.

Regarding the Dharma, is there anything to be attained? Subhūti directly perceives that it is truly non-existent; this is his attainment of correct awakening.
As for the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Dharma, he attains it within his own mind; he does not grasp at the Teacher’s Dharma as something that can be attained.
Therefore, the Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. He did not merely affirm that their words were correct;
rather, he meant that what I have attained truly resides within my own mind and does not depend on the teacher's discourse. All of this is intended to convey the meaning of non-self (*anātman*).
It is said that one attains Buddhahood by realizing it through the mind, without depending on the teacher’s discourse; only then is it considered true awakening and entry.
To attain while there is nothing to be attained is precisely what is meant by the term "Tathāgata."
Why is this? "Tathāgata" has the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, as for the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata...
Subhūti, herein there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti, that which is called "all dharmas" is not, in fact, all dharmas; it is therefore called "all dharmas."
“Subhūti, it is as if there were a person with a large body. Subhūti said, “World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person with a large body, that is precisely not a large body;
it is merely designated as a ‘large body. “Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva.
If one says, ‘I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,’ then one is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhūti...

“Bodhi” is truly not a dharma that can be called a “bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, ‘I shall adorn the buddha-fields,’ he would not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls ‘adornment of the buddha-fields’ is in fact no adornment.”
This is called adornment. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata calls him a true bodhisattva.
The Discourse on the True Son: How is it that one perceives the reason for having nothing to attain?

It is because the Tathāgata is able to thoroughly penetrate all phenomena and thereby attains non-attainment; thus, amidst the emptiness of all dharmas, he awakens to the meaning of suchness (*tathatā*).
Yunfeng said: "The meaning of 'all dharmas are suchness' (sarvadharmāḥ tathatā) is the essential purport of the Tathāgata’s teachings.
Although these dharmas consist of a thousand strands and ten thousand threads, their single, unifying principle is entirely subsumed within the two characters *ruru* (suchness-suchness).

Since 'such' (*ru*) means there is nothing that is not such, and 'suchness-suchness' (*ruru*) means there is no intentional act of being such, one speaks of the meaning of 'such' rather than 'such' itself."
Regarding the Dharma: within suchness (*tathatā*), one does not grasp at the characteristics of dharmas. As for the Tathāgata:

because there is nothing that he is not as, he is able to arise from stillness and manifest from within emptiness. It is like a mirror suspended within; there is no obstruction even as small as a hair.
Relying on the arrival of objects, he responds exactly as they arrive; when the reflected images pass, they leave no trace, yet emptiness remains.
Because its essence is thus, there is neither coming nor non-coming; even "coming" does not exist, for it is neither as it appears nor otherwise.
To say that all dharmas converge in the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) is precisely like the currents of a hundred rivers dissolving back into the great ocean:
no increase is seen, yet nothing is not accommodated. By this, one can realize the vastness encompassed by the meaning of *tathatā*. Furthermore—
How could there be a single dharma that can be named in isolation?
Your true explanation of the meaning of "tathatā" (suchness) is like this.

Yet, if there are those who say that the Tathāgata must have attained something in his perfect awakening before he is named "Tathāgata," they do not understand that the Tathāgata, in reality, has no attainment whatsoever.
Why is it seen that there is no attainment? It is because that which is attained within true nature (dharmatā) is such that nature itself is originally without phenomena (dharma).
If one takes this as a substantial basis, there is absolutely nothing to rely upon; if one sees it as empty, it is perfectly penetrating and unobstructed in every encounter.
Being neither real nor empty, where could phenomena be applied? Therefore, it is further said: "That which can be [attained] in the world..."
That which is relied upon is entirely the Dharma. Since the Dharma extends to all things, it makes no distinction between the great and the small.

Yet these "all dharmas," when approached directly, are not [ultimately real]; when their essence is realized as self-substantiated, although there are all dharmas, they are subsumed within the One Dharma.
Furthermore, as for the dharma of a single dharma, it originally possesses no dharma; thus, although one speaks of "all dharmas," they are nothing more than empty names.
How could they possibly be grasped? Therefore, it is further said that the great size of the human body is used as a metaphor for the multiplicity of all dharmas.
Yet, if this nature is not illuminated through awakening, then despite possessing a large body, it remains ultimately a hollow shell.

Furthermore, what use is there? Although all phenomena exist as metaphors, if one cannot realize them within the mind, then all phenomena are merely conventional constructs—mere imitations of a gourd.
How could they ever have arisen from within one's own fundamental nature?

This is the unique, ultimate truth. Thus, Subhūti directly stated that what the Tathāgata has described as a "vast human body" is nothing more than a mere empty name; how can such a vast body be taken as a basis for reality?

Yunfeng said: From "Thus it is" (*tathatā*) below, down to the phrase "the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-tathatārtha*), the preceding and following sections correspond to one another;
yet the metaphor used in this particular section serves as a transition, linking what precedes it with what follows.
The Discourse on the True Son: The preceding statement says there is no dharma of extinction (nirvāṇa). This is not only true of the Tathāgata;
it is likewise for the Bodhisattva. This is because the Bodhisattva penetrates the Buddha-nature, differing from the Buddha by only a single interval.
If a Bodhisattva were to say, "I shall transform and deliver immeasurable sentient beings," this would be clinging to...
The method of transformation and deliverance cannot be designated as that of a bodhisattva. For those who are deluded are sentient beings, while those who have attained awakening are bodhisattvas.
To regard others as sentient beings and to regard oneself as a bodhisattva is precisely the mark of the self and others (pudgala-dṛṣṭi).
How could there be the stage of a bodhisattva while the four marks still persist? Therefore, it is further said: "The Buddha has no person."
This is the mark of a self, a sentient being, or a life-span. To speak of a "Buddha" allows us to know that the Bodhisattva does not fall into the dharma of transformation and deliverance.
Therefore, the Tathāgata further said: Since the Bodhisattva does not harbor a mind of transformation and deliverance, their mind may be known as pure.
However, if a Bodhisattva were to have a mind that seeks purity, this very mind would itself constitute purity.
[The Bodhisattva] is thus constrained. Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not say, "I have already adorned the Buddha-land.
This is because once the mind has reached the state of adornment, one has already cast off the traces of adornment;
it is simply beyond naming, yet is forcibly named "adornment. In reality, what is there to be adorned? Thus, furthermore—

He said: "If a bodhisattva perceives that both the dharma of transformation and the dharma of adornment are characterized by emptiness, then they know that this body is not a body and these dharmas are not dharmas;
they have thus attained penetration into the dharma of non-self. This is truly what is called a bodhisattva."
Yunfeng said: "While all dharmas are taught, he specifically brings forth the dharma of giving.
To say that he teaches all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, yet singles out the dharma of transformation and deliverance, is to say it is for the sake of Bodhisattvas.

Above, the six dusts were mentioned, yet only the characteristic of form was discussed, because sound, fragrance, and so forth arise from form. Here, the four marks are mentioned, yet only [the mark of]..."
There is no self-dharma. This is because humans, sentient beings, and life-spanners all arise from the notion of a "self.
To preach the dharma of non-self and call one a "thoroughly realized" person means to be thoroughly versed in this and reach that [beyond it].

When there is no obstruction between this and that, it is simply the single mind of perfect enlightenment; what room is there for anything to exist as a "dharma"? It is at this point that non-self is preached. Not...
When he speaks of the mind yet refers to "dharmas," this is the Tathāgata pointing out the locus of the bodhisattva’s dharma of emptiness;
it is not a statement that all dharmas are utterly non-existent, for he further leaves behind the single dharma of non-self, causing later generations to harbor doubt.
Chapter Eighteen: The Section on the Single Essence Viewed as Identical Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*)? “It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)? “It is so, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti, does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
“Thus it is, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye? “Thus it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?”
"No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.

My son speaks truly. Although the preceding passage stated that there is no self (*anātman*), the reason for questioning this again by means of the five eyes is precisely because the Tathāgata does not preach a doctrine of total extinction.
For the eye is also one of the faculties within my own body; it is without self.

The body should then be empty of the characteristics of the eye. One who does not know the characteristic of non-self is free from the burden of the body, yet it is not that the body itself is absent.
When the burdens of this body are entirely forgotten, the wisdom-nature of the self then permeates through the light of the eyes;
thus there are these five eyes. The Tathāgata’s inquiry into the five eyes explains the profound in a single step.
A single step. Subhūti’s answer regarding the five eyes is such that each step sees one step higher; both are points of mutual correspondence, needle meeting needle.
As for the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*): it is the eye of the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*). Since humans possess a physical body, they are endowed with this eye;
yet there are differences such as being blind or squinting, and distinctions such as clarity or dimness. This holds true until one possesses the full power of vision.
That one sees what is correct and the other sees what is erroneous—this is why their physical eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) differ so vastly.
Ordinary people and the Tathāgata share these same eyes; yet, because the Tathāgata possesses them, he is able to realize the supreme fruit through these very eyes.

Thus, it is appropriate to call this the "fleshly eye" of the Tathāgata. As for the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*), it refers to the fact that the scope of his visual faculty is exceedingly vast. And...
One can see all sentient beings universally; there is nothing that does not enter one's sight.

Whether it be good or evil, deviant or correct, just as when looking down from a high vantage point, even the finest hair is seen in its entirety. This is obtained through the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) after attaining the fruits of realization.
As for the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), its visual power is exceedingly clear, enabling one to perceive the past and future lives of all sentient beings within a single flash of wisdom-light.
Illumination: all nine types are entirely clear and transparent, without anything that can be obscured or embellished;

this is perceived through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which is precisely the greatness of seeing and the clarity of vision. As for the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*), whatever it beholds is uniformly governed by the Dharma.

One sees the correct and does not see the deviant; one sees the good and does not see the evil. Thus, my greatness lies in clearly perceiving that all things return to the same source through myriad virtues.
As for the Buddha-eye, it perceives that all sentient beings in the world can attain Buddhahood, without any distinction between good and evil.
This is precisely opening one’s eyes to have compassion for sentient beings, and closing one’s eyes to bring them all to completion.
The Dharma-realm; there is nothing that does not enter its eye. This is a general outline of the five eyes. Yunfeng said: "The five eyes are one eye.
When analyzed separately, they have degrees of depth; when integrated, they have no high or low.
The Tathāgata possesses the five eyes, and ordinary people likewise possess the five eyes. As for the point of distinction between them, it is simply..."
This begins with the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). If explained according to the latter four eyes, this interpretation remains incomplete;
it may be further elucidated as follows. As for the fleshly eye: where there is a physical body, there is this eye.

The fleshly eye of the body constitutes a single faculty, yet it is the eye alone that communicates with the mind. Therefore, the mind’s deviation or rectitude is manifested solely through the eyes. The eyes—
That which is seen by it causes the mind to be constantly drawn toward those objects. If the mind does not abide in emptiness, the eyes will become attached to forms;

therefore, these are called "fleshly eyes" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). However, the Tathāgata’s fleshly eye is able to perceive the arising and ceasing of his own body, and thus differs from the eyes of ordinary beings.
This particular eye was acquired after the attainment of his physical body, and it arises and ceases simultaneously with that body.

This is simply because it cannot serve as a basis for reliance. However, with a single eye, the Tathāgata perceives that his own birth comes from this and his cessation goes from this, without any confusion or obscuration;
therefore, he must necessarily enter through the gateway of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).

As for the "heavenly eye" (*divya-cakṣus*), one borrows the term "heaven" to describe its greatness—it is merely high and far-reaching. It is like a person looking toward the sky with their eyes, yet not [being able to see it].
It can exhaust the limits of Heaven. Heaven gazes upon humanity with its eyes and is able to perceive all the subtleties of human beings because it is great.
Being great, there is nowhere it does not pervade; being high, there is nowhere it does not illuminate; being far-reaching, there is nowhere it does not reach.
The Tathāgata is able to possess this eye, whereby he can pervade the realms of the ten directions and penetrate them with a single glance;
this is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). As for the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*), its brilliance is sufficient to illuminate the obscure, examine the subtle, and discern even the finest hairs.
The Tathāgata possesses the light of wisdom of the three periods of time within his eyes; thus, he does not merely see himself alone.
Regarding its arising and ceasing, departing and coming; it is able to perceive the various physical forms and characteristics of sentient beings.
Because its radiance must illuminate them—just as the brilliance of the sun and moon necessarily shines—it is called the "eye of wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*). As for the "dharma-eye" (*dharma-cakṣus*):
that which is seen by this eye is entirely in accord with the Dharma, ensuring that un-Dharmic matters can no longer cause delusion. Thus, the Tathāgata once [employed] the dharma-eye.
To discern the Asuras’ feigned path that confuses truth with falsehood, and to enable them to turn away from Māra and enter the Right Path—all these are attained through the Dharma-eye.
As for the Buddha-eye, it is because whatever is seen by this eye is everywhere the Buddha.
Toward all sentient beings, one can give rise to great compassion through the eyes, ensuring that there are none among them who do not attain Buddhahood.
At the mere glance of the Buddha-eye, they immediately realize Bodhi; this is what is meant by "opening the eyes is itself the deliverance of the world."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River truly called ‘sand’ by the Buddha?
“Indeed, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata calls them ‘sand. “Subhūti, what do you think?
If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and if one were to take the number of grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers...”
“Would these realms be many? “Very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Within all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all minds are ‘not-minds’; they are called ‘minds. Why is this so, Subhūti? Because the past mind does not exist...”
It can be attained. The present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
Your words are truly spoken. As stated above, one who is endowed with the five eyes can see the minds of all people, yet there is nothing that is not seen even by that which is "non-mind.
Therefore, following the discussion of the five eyes, three kinds of mind are explained in order to demonstrate this non-mind.
It is not that there are none who cannot see; it is simply that the Ganges River is mentioned by way of its sands, and a single river is mentioned by way of its grains of sand.
The number of rivers is like the number of sands. Through these repeated and winding turns, the point is entirely to speak of the vastness of the Buddha-worlds.
It is said that wherever there is a world, there must be a Buddha residing therein; thus, the multitude of worlds corresponds to the [multitude of] Buddhas.
As numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand—this means that the entire world is filled with Buddhas;
therefore, it is called a Buddha-world. A Buddha-world is a world entirely sustained by the Buddhas.
For every single world, there is a portion sustained by a single Buddha. Thus it extends to all worlds.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) refers to that which sustains and presides [over it]. There are also Buddhas therein; this means that in every single place throughout the world, there is a Buddha.
If one examines the phrase "within those lands," one will know that this is precisely the teaching of dividing the world in order to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Now, where there is a world, there are lands; where there are lands, there are people. Where there are...
A person possesses various minds; within the human mind there are many types of minds.
Thus, one knows that while the mind is one, its types are not one. This is why the two characters "several" (若干) are used.

That the Tathāgata, through the clarity of his five eyes, knows them all completely, is precisely because although these several minds differ from one another, in their true nature they are simply called "non-mind."
This is because all states of mind belong to subsequent arising; they are by no means the pure original nature.
How, then, can they be considered "mind"? Why is it that they are not the mind? It is because the human mind consists of only three aspects: past, present, and future.
Since these three cannot be definitively grasped, yet the human mind inevitably involves them—just as [the following example].
Coming specifically to this place, one sees that it is not the mind; this is precisely what is meant by being fully endowed with the five eyes.
Yunfeng said: "The past, present, and future need not be viewed as former lives, this life, and future lives.
Take even a single matter or a single word: the moment it leaves the mouth, it is the past; the words themselves are the present."
The present; that which has not yet been spoken of is the future. All are contained within a single moment; when explained, they cannot be divided into before and after.
These three lines of the sutra are profoundly significant. Previously, it was asked how many kinds of mind there are;
here, only three types of mind are discussed because one sees that no mind exists outside of these three. As for the past mind: this matter has already passed, and this mind...
To "linger" means to possess much attachment and a sense of cherishing. Therefore, once this mind lingers, one remains deluded for a lifetime.
As for the "present mind," it is like wealth, nobility, poverty, or low status—each has its own station, and one must not overstep that station in pursuit of something else.
People simply fail to see through their current situation and instead believe that what they occupy is their true self.
If one remains long in this state, a mind of attachment will arise. Furthermore, if one thinks, "That which I occupy here is merely temporary," a mind of weariness with the constant will again arise.
Therefore, while in the present, one does not recognize it as being present. As for the future, since this realm is not before one's eyes, one merely posits a possibility.
One conceives this object as still being in the future, yet forms an anticipatory thought; thus, one gives rise to many anxieties over gain and loss.
If it is eventually obtained in the future, it opens the door to fortune-seeking; if it is ultimately not obtained in the future, it further opens the gate to resentment.
When the Tathāgata spoke of the "three things that cannot be obtained," it was for this reason.

This indirect deliberation is truly like speech that cuts through nails and chews through iron. Therefore, its power to shatter the non-enlightened minds of sentient beings is also exceedingly decisive.
Yunfeng further said: "The present mind is fundamentally not separate from the affairs of daily life, such as eating and drinking; it is simply that..."
Why is it that the mind arises again and again yet lacks self-mastery? It is because people, in their present state, are frequently dissatisfied;

thus, they cannot attain mastery. When the Tathāgata speaks of the present mind, he originally intends for people to seek fulfillment within the present themselves, yet instead they abandon the present to seek it in the distant future.
If one understands this, then one knows that both the past and the future are likewise [unattainable].
From the present locus, one gives rise to the perception of the distant. For example, when the body is situated here, this is the present;
yet, even with this, one considers it insufficient, further reaching back into the past and projecting forward into the future, such that the present itself becomes ungraspable.
This is how the present mind gives rise to minds of the past and the future.

This is the general outline. Regarding the word "attaining" (*de*), there is also an interpretation: what is discussed here as "attaining" refers entirely to that which is absolutely unattainable, yet is sought with great effort.
This is like the Confucian saying that attainment depends on destiny (*ming*); it is the doctrine that seeking is of no benefit for attaining.
Chapter Nineteen: The Universal Transformation of the Dharma Realm.

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? “It would be so, World-Honored One; that person would [acquire much merit].”
For this reason, the merit obtained is exceedingly great. Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one obtains much merit;
because merit is non-substantial, the Tathāgata says that one obtains much merit.

Zizhen’s Explanation: The preceding statement that the mind cannot be apprehended in this manner implies that merit is inherently possessed within the nature of the self; thus, it can be attained naturally without seeking.
The Tathāgata also spoke of it in terms of non-apprehension, not meaning that merit is fundamentally non-existent. Since merit resides within the nature, it is attained without seeking. Merit...
Virtue lies in giving; yet, having attained it, one returns to non-attainment. This is another profound layer of meaning of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he asks Subhūti whether, by practicing such giving, one obtains merit.
Within these causal conditions, there appears to be a measure of "obtaining little" versus "obtaining much. If the giving is great, the merit obtained is likewise great. Then...
Merit follows the act of giving; what has it to do with one's nature? Therefore, he speaks of the single word "reality" (*sat*).
Now, if merit resides in one's virtuous nature, it is empty; if it resides in giving, it is real.
Being real, its causal conditions can be measured, and thus the abundance of that merit is likewise limited. For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke the word "one" (*eka*) to demonstrate this.
The abundance of merit arises merely from the perspective formed by my words; it is not that there are actually any traces of such abundance.
Yunfeng said: "If it exists, it is real; if it does not exist, it is empty. Merit is not an object that comes from without. Why?
Therefore, we speak of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). This is because merit originally possesses seeds, which constitute the causes and conditions.
"Cause" refers to that which persists from the past. In all matters, there must first be a cause before conditions can arise based upon it.
Furthermore, within these causes, there are two aspects: when one follows a good cause, good conditions arise; when one follows an evil cause, evil conditions likewise arise.
This point merely speaks of virtuous causes and conditions, precisely because the nature of merit is fundamentally good.
Since the nature of goodness is innate, how could there be any admixture of evil? It simply takes the single aspect of giving as the foundation for cultivating virtue;
it is not a matter of comparing the quantity of what is given, but rather that with every act of giving, one accordingly receives merit. This is merit.
Since even virtue cannot be apprehended, how could one wish to apprehend that which is not the mind? One should fix one’s gaze upon the concluding sentence.
Chapter Twenty: Detachment from Form and Characteristics.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of his perfected physical body? “No, World-Honored One.”
One should not see the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body (*rūpakāya*). Why is this?

What the Tathāgata calls the perfection of the physical body is itself not the perfection of the physical body; it is merely designated as the "perfection of the physical body. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the perfection of the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*)? "No, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the perfection..."
[They] perceive various marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata says that being endowed with all marks is itself not being endowed [with them]; it is merely called "being endowed with all marks.
My son, you have spoken truly. As for what was said above—that since merit is non-existent, its nature is fundamentally empty—yet the physical body (rūpakāya) is nonetheless severed [and ceases].
One may indeed grasp at signs. The "form-body" (*rūpakāya*) refers to the physical body. "Complete" means that the five limbs are without deficiency.
The Buddha possesses five limbs, and sentient beings likewise possess five limbs; this statement implies that the Buddha’s body subsumes the bodies of sentient beings.
For now, let us not merely discuss the Buddha’s marks of completeness, but rather take up the completeness of sentient beings themselves.
When one realizes this through direct experience, one knows that any sentient being who possesses the marks of perfection is a Buddha.
Therefore, can it be said that a Buddha may be seen by means of a physical body free from all deficiencies?

If one says that such marks exist and that those who see them will necessarily give rise to a heart of joy and reach the ultimate, this body is not separate from the physical body; it nonetheless returns to [the source].

How can it be that while this physical body perishes, this nature remains forever? Knowing that the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is fundamentally unreliable, it is said that "it is not a complete form-body.
This is merely because it possesses form that it is given a provisional name. Therefore, it is further stated:
"As for my present body, it possesses the thirty-two marks; these are what is called the perfection of all marks."
Whoever beholds them does not fail to give rise to a heart of reverent gazing.
However, as for my own possession of the various marks, they do not exist apart from this physical body; since even this has its end, how could one possibly cling to them?

Therefore, although it is said that there are the thirty-two marks of perfection, in reality they do not exist; they are merely given strong designations. These two sections speak of their possession.
This is a distinction regarding the marks of the feet.
Yunfeng said: "When the marks are fully complete, one is called a perfect person. However, if the appearance is complete while the nature is not, one is not someone who has fulfilled their form.
How is this different from one whose official rank is incomplete? Thus did the Tathāgata speak to the assembly.
Having already stated that the physical marks of birth are not to be relied upon, it follows that even the thirty-two marks lack any basis for reliance.
Their essential purport ultimately leads to formlessness (*animitta*), and by extension, one can know that they lead to the absence of dharmas (*anātmadharma*).
Therefore, the subsequent passage clarifies this very point through the doctrine of the non-existence of dharmas.
Venerable Ānanda said: This section concludes by tracing the character "Buddha" back to its full presence within sentient beings.
Thus, one perceives the self-nature of seeing and form within sentient beings, as well as among the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all the way up to the Tathāgata.

All these are physical bodies that cannot be relied upon; thus, the principle of formlessness is established. Although this treatise was previously discussed in the middle [section], it shall be recorded again here.
Section Twenty-one: On That Which Is Not Spoken of as Being Spoken.
Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall preach some dharma. Do not have such a thought. Why is this?
If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has preached some dharma, they would be slandering the Buddha, because they would not understand what I have taught.
Subhūti, one who preaches the Dharma has no dharma to preach; it is called the preaching of the Dharma. At that time...
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "They are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Subhūti, as for 'sentient beings, sentient beings,' the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; they are merely designated as 'sentient beings.'"
The Discourse on the True Son: The preceding section spoke of signlessness; this section speaks of the non-existence of dharmas.
This is because, since the characteristics of dharmas arise through mutual dependence, those characteristics must be empty, and thus all dharmas are also empty. This is why the Tathāgata said:
"Do not think that before I had preached the Dharma, I first conceived a single thought, thinking, 'I shall now preach the Dharma. Had I, prior to preaching the Dharma..."

If one first forms the thought, "I am being constrained by the Dharma," then those who hear my Dharma should likewise not first form the thought upon hearing it, thinking, "The Tathāgata is about to preach the Dharma, and I shall now hear it.
If a person were to form such a thought, they would be one who does not know the Buddha; how then could they understand the Buddha?

Regarding the meaning of what has been taught, those who call it "slandering the Buddha" do so because they fail to clarify the great purport of the sutra and instead merely become confused by the secondary details of its phrasing.
Yunfeng said: "The upper character 'nian' (念) refers to the Tathāgata’s own mindfulness; the lower character 'nian' refers to..."
This question concerns the thoughts of sentient beings. Furthermore, it refers to those who merely rely on the words and phrases of the scriptures, reciting and explaining them.
Your true teaching is as follows:
since the Tathāgata has stated that both the one who preaches the Dharma and the one who hears the Dharma are without any dharma that can be apprehended.
If one relies [on such things], what basis will there be for future generations to follow and believe?
This is why Subhūti asks again. To address him as "Subhūti" while adding the two characters "Huìmìng" (Wisdom-Life) indicates that at this moment, Subhūti has already attained the life of wisdom.
Yunfeng said: "The life-force of wisdom (*hui-ming*) is precisely the nature of wisdom (*hui-xing*). Within this nature, wisdom is inherently present;
this wisdom emerges from the life-force of the nature and does not arise subsequently through conditions. Thus, life-force is itself wisdom; they cannot be divided into two separate items."
It is precisely because life-force (*ming*) is not wisdom that there is no way to perceive the nature; it is because wisdom is not life-force that there is no means to clarify the mind.
Therefore, wisdom and life-force must be unified. If one speaks of wisdom alone, it pertains to subsequent arising rather than primordial awakening.
Only when wisdom is contained within the nature does it arise together with birth and not perish together with extinction; this is because it is the very nature itself. At such a time...
"Subhūti has already attained perfect awakening; it is for this reason that he is so named.
This was the true teaching of the Son [of the Buddha]. At that time, Subhūti again asked the Tathāgata:
"In this future age, there will be sentient beings for whom there is no dharma to be taught and no dharma to be heard; yet, could there be anyone among them who is able to believe in the Tathāgata?"
"No. The Tathāgata says that these sentient beings all possess Buddha-nature; they cannot be designated by the name 'sentient beings,' nor can they be designated as 'non-sentient beings.

That sentient beings are called 'sentient beings' is merely because they have not yet realized the fruit of Buddhahood and have not yet reached the other shore; thus they are forcibly designated by the name 'sentient beings. In reality, however, [they are not]."
Birth is immeasurable; why then do you categorize it all under the term "sentient beings"?
Yunfeng said: "Neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings—this is the place where the Tathāgata transforms and enlightens sentient beings."

Among the various modes of birth—egg, womb, moisture, and transformation—there are those who undergo transformation and cast off their ordinary physical forms. Once one has cast off this ordinary form, one has reached the shore;
therefore, it is said that they are "not sentient beings. To say they are "not sentient beings" implies there are still traces of sentient beings remaining;
to say they are "not non-sentient beings" means even the name of "sentient being" is forgotten. Thus, the subsequent passage does not mention "sentient beings," and...
This refers directly to the bodhicitta.
○ Chapter Twenty-Two: There is No Dharma to be Attained.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
"Is it that there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti.
In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained that could be called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

The True Discourse on the Son: This section shows that the Tathāgata, regarding the nature of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), returns entirely to emptiness without leaving even a hair’s breadth behind.
He did this so that future generations might rely upon this to understand that the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is distinct from that of ordinary people.
Therefore, Subhūti [states] that the nature of perfect enlightenment is truly unattainable; the Tathāgata simply takes it as such.
To say that this is the nature of perfect enlightenment is to claim it is not attained through dharmas. This disregards the fact that all dharmas must be dissolved;
were even the slightest trace of a dharma to remain within it, it would no longer be the true enlightened nature.
Yunfeng said: This section emphasizes only the phrase "there is not even the slightest dharma that can be obtained.
Seeing that the Tathāgata does not retain a single dharma is, in fact, to penetrate all dharmas. The dharmas are external; awakening is within the mind.
If one were to awaken to my mind by means of external dharmas, there would be both awakening and non-awakening. Therefore, it is said: "there is not even the slightest dharma that can be obtained."
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Section on Purifying the Mind and Practicing Goodness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By means of being without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
He immediately attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, that which is called "wholesome dharmas" by the Tathāgata is not, in fact, wholesome dharmas;
it is merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."
The Discourse on the Reality of the Son: The preceding statement said that there is no dharma that can be taught; here, it further speaks of wholesome dharmas.

This is precisely because one perceives that all dharmas converge in the same way, without any distinction of high or low; therefore, another section is spoken concerning the exposition of wholesome dharmas.
The Tathāgata stated that this dharma is ineffable because its nature is profoundly level and impartial, and furthermore—
Because they are equal and without distinction, there is no difference of high or low among them.
It is precisely because this unsurpassed, right, and perfect enlightenment mind arises and is equally possessed by all.
Yunfeng said: "Are there distinctions between the two characters 'ping' (level/even) and 'deng' (equal)? If one were to say they are identical, then everything would be the same.
Yet, if they are equal, there must be differentiation. For example, consider the Tathāgata and Subhūti and all the other Bodhisattvas;

they are all people within the stage of Buddhahood. Nevertheless, why are their names and forms distinguished here? From this, it can be seen that within 'ping' (levelness), there is 'deng' (equality)."
Furthermore, if one speaks of this awakening as extending upward, then all bodhisattvas share this same awakened nature with the Tathāgata;
if one speaks of it as extending downward, then all sentient beings likewise possess this same awakened nature as the Tathāgata.
Within this equality, there is no talk of high or low. There is also another interpretation of the two characters "equality" (pingdeng).
These two lines still only speak of the Dharma; they never speak of persons. It is merely that the Dharma is divided into high and low according to the person.
In reality, the two characters "equality" (pingdeng) are identical to the two characters "middle way" (zhongyong) in Confucianism.

This is because it says that this Dharma is originally without the extraordinary and is exceedingly level; it also has no classifications and possesses no grades. Even if those of later generations were as wise as...
If the ignorant were to hear and see this together, they would not resort to heterodox views or deviant paths to destroy this Dharma of equality.
This commentary focuses exclusively on the two characters "equality" (pingdeng), while the meaning of the subsequent phrase is self-evident.
The Discourse on the True Son: This enlightened nature alone is equally possessed by every person. Thus, those who have first awakened ought to awaken those who awaken later;
how, then, could the four marks of self and others exist? Therefore it is said: "There are no four marks.
Since there are no marks, all that constitutes the Dharma is the goodness of the enlightened nature; one may simply call it "wholesome dharmas" (śubhadharma).

Dharmas have no inherent goodness; they are good by virtue of their nature. If one clings to the idea that the Tathāgata definitively taught dharmas, or becomes attached to wholesome dharmas, one then falls into the conceptualization of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that they are "not wholesome dharmas," being merely empty names.
Yunfeng said: "If one speaks of 'wholesome dharmas' as referring to the goodness within awakened nature, then goodness is still not being discussed in terms of the dharmas themselves.
Section Twenty-Four: The Inconceivable Equality of Merit and Wisdom.

Subhūti, if someone were to take all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and offer such a heap of the seven precious jewels as a gift, and if another person were to take this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra—
Even if one were to accept, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse, the former merit would not equal a hundredth part of it;
it would not equal a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
The Master Zhen said: "He spoke of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), and further traced them back to giving (*dāna*).
Having spoken of giving, he again returned to upholding and explaining [the teachings]. Thus, it is from wholesome dharmas that they are linked together. Furthermore, the Tathāgata said:
'If there were people in the world who could gather the seven great treasures of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, into one place, and with..."
One may perform acts of giving that could be called abundant; yet in the end, they do not equal the superior merit of receiving, upholding, and explaining [this teaching].
This is because all such acts of giving derive their excellence from this Dharma. Therefore it is said:
"A hundredth part does not come close; even a hundred-thousand-millionth part, or any calculation or analogy, cannot reach it."
This is simply to clarify his wholesome dharmas in general.
Yunfeng said: "The previous statement used the Ganges River as a metaphor for giving; this statement uses Mount Sumeru as a metaphor for giving.
The former spoke of its abundance; this speaks of its magnitude. As for "accumulation," it refers to gathering all that exists under heaven.
The seven treasures are in one place, yet they do not distinguish between what belongs to oneself and what belongs to others; this passage of the sutra seems to express this meaning.
Furthermore, it says that its true essence is explained through the two characters "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*). Thus, one can see the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the sutra:
starting from the phrase "the equality of dharmas" up to the section "it is not an ordinary person," all is due to non-attachment.
The Dharma can be spoken; thus, a series of questions and answers concerning the arising of wholesome dharmas is produced.

From the section below on "the phrases of ordinary beings" onward, it is again through the speakability of signlessness that a series of questions and answers concerning the "mark of total integration" (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*) is produced.
Chapter Twenty-Five: The Transformation of Those Not to Be Transformed.
