Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? Because, in reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a "self," it is not a self; yet ordinary people think that there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called ordinary beings by the Tathāgata are, in truth, not ordinary beings; they are merely designated as "ordinary beings.
My son, you have directly explained that the excellence of the meaning of this sutra is such that the Tathāgata [has taught] this sutra for this purpose.
The Tathāgata has delivered many across [to liberation]. Yet the Tathāgata further says:
"Do not think that when I preach this sutra today, I conceive even a single thought that my preaching of the sutra is solely for the purpose of delivering sentient beings of future generations.

If one were to harbor such a thought—that one delivers sentient beings by means of this—then although the Dharma may be excellent, one still maintains the mark of a self (*ātman*). Indeed, [this is so because...]

To preach the sutras while holding to a self, or to preach the sutras while holding to a self and use those sutras to save others, is for the Buddha to regard himself as a sentient being and to regard others as sentient beings;

what then would there be to save? Therefore, he established the question of "no-self" so that those who receive, uphold, explain, and interpret [the teachings] in future generations shall all be without self. If one explains them for others while still harboring [a sense of self], [it is not true liberation].
I am but an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). For the mind of an ordinary person originally intends to save others and provide explanations;
yet, they merely claim that this sutra is not something they cannot recite, nor is it something they cannot explain.

This is precisely not the intent with which the Tathāgata preached the sutra—how could such a person be anything other than an ordinary person? To say that one is "attached to the matter" truly means being attached to the act of saving others.
This is the way of human affairs. However, if one speaks of "ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana), there must necessarily be something that stands in contrast to them;

thus, the mark of a self (ātman) arises once again. Therefore, it is said that "ordinary being" is merely a provisional designation (prajñapti); there is no such thing as an ordinary being in reality.
Yunfeng said: "Ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are not merely a class of fools. Because they have not yet transcended the mundane to enter the sacred, they are called ordinary people.
One must not view them as shallow; the Tathāgata has provided these sections specifically so that people may uphold, recite, and explain them."
To instead take "ordinary people" (*pṛthagjana*) as referring to those of future generations—how could such a principle exist?
It is simply that for one who has already transcended the world, after having transcended it, there remains no further name or form of "transcending the world" within the mind.

This is just as the Tathāgata regards later generations: not forming the thought of them as ordinary people transcending the world is itself the entry into the stage of the sages (*āryabhūmi*). This section...
This is the Tathāgata borrowing his own [body] as an analogy for later people; it must not be treated as a mere empty "head-word" (hua-tou).
Chapter Twenty-Six: The Dharma-body is Without Characteristics.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti...

"It is so, it is so. One should view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage king would also be a Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks."
Come. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who see me by means of form, or seek me by means of sound, these people follow a perverted path; they cannot perceive the Tathāgata."

Yunfeng said: This section again uses physical characteristics (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) to explain the matter repeatedly, all in order to inspire Subhūti to realize the state of the "single integration" (*ekapiṇḍa*).
It follows from what was previously stated that the thirty-two marks cannot be perceived.

This further question regarding "being able to see" is precisely because the Tathāgata intended for Subhūti to recognize that he must not see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks (*rūpalakṣaṇa*). Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is.

This was an occasion that welcomed the Tathāgata’s intent, as his vision was different from that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*). Here, "wheel" refers to the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Furthermore, although this wheel of Dharma exists, there is no one to turn it; for they do not realize that the wheel can carry one far.

Thus, the merit lies in the one who is able to turn it. Even a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the marks of a Tathāgata and is further able to transform and govern a nation through the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
yet in truth, he has never relied upon the existence of these marks as a cause [for his success].

One practices the Dharma of the Tathāgata. If one were to say that one practices this Dharma merely because of possessing [physical] marks, how would a noble wheel-turning king differ from a Tathāgata?
Therefore, it is said that he is "the Tathāgata," yet this does not mean he is truly identical to a Tathāgata.
To clarify this through the teaching of the four-line verse, one sees that both form and sound fall within the realm of marks (*nimitta*) and must not be clung to.

How can one seek to see or hear by means of this desire? If one seeks to see merely through these forms and seeks to hear merely through these sounds, one loses the Tathāgata’s essential principle of true emptiness and formlessness.
One will mistakenly enter onto a heterodox path, and those who practice in such a manner do not follow the orthodox teaching; how then could they perceive the true countenance of the Tathāgata?
This section is a pivotal point of resolution within the sutra. In brief, the four lines regarding the absence of self-characteristics are elucidated through each of these four lines;
furthermore, the subsequent four-line verse is likewise illuminated by this very point.
Yunfeng further said: "The previous statement regarding 'seeing the Tathāgata' was the Tathāgata causing Subhūti to fix his gaze with one eye;
this current statement regarding 'contemplating the Tathāgata' is the Tathāgata causing Subhūti to focus his mind with single-minded intent.
The former refers to the external, while the latter refers to the internal; such is the difference in the interpretation of these two characters."

Chapter Twenty-seven: On Neither Annihilation nor Extinction Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the marks of physical perfection, Subhūti, do not think so.
The Tathāgata did not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the marks of physical perfection.

Therefore, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, if you should think that those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* advocate the annihilation of all phenomena, do not hold such a thought.
Why is this? One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the mark of annihilation regarding phenomena.
My son, you have spoken truly.
This section of question and answer emphasizes only the three characters "annihilation" (*duanmie xiang*). Since the Tathāgata is already endowed with...
This mark does not exist by means of a single mark alone; therefore, there is nowhere it is not fully present.
Thus, it is said that one does not attain the mind of perfect enlightenment through the mark of fullness.

For the mind of perfect enlightenment does not rely upon marks, yet it specifically employs the fullness of marks to realize the vision of this mind. Those who possess this mind do not yet have its marks.
If one does not possess the mind of ultimate *samyaksambodhi*, how could there be any marks?
Therefore, it is further taught that the mark of cessation is used as proof; yet, in reality, even this mark of cessation cannot be apprehended and is merely a name.
Yunfeng said: "The mark of annihilation does not mean cutting off the roots and severing the stalks.
If it were severed yet remained connected, or extinguished yet truly arose, this would merely depict a scene of empty stillness by leaving not a single dharma behind.
If it were ultimately annihilated such that not a single dharma could be transmitted, how could that be the Tathāgata’s guidance?"
Yunfeng further said: "People only know that the teachings of the Śākya school are empty and hollow;

how could they know that the Tathāgata’s discourse on 'true emptiness and formlessness' is actually achieved through genuine, foundational practice, reaching the very pinnacle before true emptiness is attained?"

It is signless. This is like the three characters "not severed," "not destroyed," and "extinguished. These are the Tathāgata’s means of leading people onto the great path, so that each may realize their own enlightened nature.
If this Dharma were subject to severance, destruction, or extinction, how could one cause people to believe in, accept, and uphold it?
Only through non-interruption does the Dharma naturally share the same beginning and end as heaven and earth. Heaven and earth...
The rotation never ceases; the non-interruption of this Dharma is likewise so.
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, it truly reaches the point of the simile of "suspended needles measuring shadows."
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Section on Non-Attachment and Non-Greed.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River and offer them as a gift;

If, moreover, there should be someone who, knowing that all dharmas are without self, attains the stage of patience (kṣānti), this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattvas. Why is this? Subhūti, it is because these bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?
“Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be grasped with attachment; for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.”
Yunfeng said: "In this passage, one must focus on the phrase: 'Attaining non-self, one achieves patience.
Receiving merit and performing merit each have their own distinctions. The character 'receive' (shou) corresponds to the preceding two characters 'bestow' (shi);

because of what is bestowed, one obtains what is received. The character 'perform' (zuo) again corresponds to the preceding character 'receive'; because of what is received, one perceives what is performed."
This section further employs the topic of giving as an illustration. It demonstrates that the perfection of patience is superior to giving;
the Tathāgata stated that the merit received by one who achieves patience is far more excellent than that of such giving.
This is because patience is the essential key to entering the path to enlightenment, wherein the realization of non-self arises spontaneously.
In the cultivation of study, the capacity for endurance (*kṣānti*) is predominant. It is because people cannot endure that they fail to achieve success.
One does not realize that the mind free from self (*anātman*) is precisely what allows one to realize *bodhi*; all such realizations are accomplished through endurance.

Therefore, it is said that "all phenomena are without self" (*sarvadharma-anātman*). The phrase "accomplished through endurance" (*kṣāntyā siddhaḥ*) should be read as a single unit. [The preceding...]
It is said that giving belongs to sentient beings, and this, in turn, belongs to the bodhisattva. This does not mean that the bodhisattva departs from giving;
rather, it is precisely through this that one realizes the bodhicitta.
The True Discourse on the Son: For what reason is it said? It is because of that which is attained. Why is this superior to what preceded it?
It is because that which is attained is inherently possessed by me; it does not depend on external arrival, nor is it a case of one gift resulting in one reception.
Thus it is said that the Bodhisattva does not accept merit. "Does not accept" does not mean that he is given something and then returns it.
It is not received. That which belongs to me was not bestowed by another; where could it possibly be contained as something received?
Therefore, it is called "not received. Yunfeng said: "That which is given to me and yet not received is an external thing; though one receives it, there is no room for it."
The "receiver" is one's own nature. Since merit is this very nature, it cannot be increased or diminished; from what, then, could it be received? Therefore, it is further said:
"A bodhisattva should not be greedily attached to the merit they have performed. Merit is created by oneself and received by oneself.
In reality, if one takes this as 'mine' and seeks more of it, then that is greed. Greed...
Thus, there has never been anyone who does not become attached to signs. The reason for this is that it all arises from the mind that desires to receive [phenomena].
This is why the Bodhisattva does not receive them. Furthermore, the two characters "greed" (貪) and "attachment" (著) differ from the explanations of greed, anger, and delusion (貪瞋癡).
This character "greed" (貪) refers to those who are directed toward the realization of the supreme fruit; it must be understood through direct experience.

Since the preceding [discussions] all distinguish [phenomena] by way of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), one should know that the conditioned (saṃskṛta) sphere is likewise greed—that is, attachment to the conditioned.
Only by examining it in this manner can one enter into the subtle details.

Chapter Twenty-nine: On the Tranquility of Dignified Conduct Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere, nor does he go anywhere; therefore [he is called the Tathāgata].
The Tathāgata’s son has spoken the truth:
that which was previously stated as being "not to be greedily attached to" refers especially to the characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa), to which one must not be attached.
Therefore, the Tathāgata said: "In this world, I cannot be defined by coming or going, sitting or lying down. If one were to...
People say that if the Tathāgata comes, he exists as a form characterized by physical appearance; they say that if he goes, he exists as a characteristic of empty extinction;
and they say that if he sits or lies down, he exists as a characteristic of coming and going within the world.
This is to perceive the Tathāgata through his marks, and thus they fail to understand the meaning of what is taught regarding the Tathāgata. How can this be seen?
The reason this is not understood is that the Tathāgata is neither existent nor non-existent.
As for his coming, he truly comes from nowhere; as for his going, he truly goes nowhere. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Yunfeng said: This section borrows the four characters "going," "coming," "sitting," and "lying" as metaphors for its intended meaning.
On each of these four characters, there is the word "as if" (ru), which reveals that going, coming, sitting, and lying do not truly exist.
It is merely spoken for the sake of those later generations who rely on walls and lean against them. People believe only in the Tathāgata as having form and color.
When a person suddenly conceives a thought of "coming," they perceive it as coming, and the practice of gazing upon, prostrating to, and reverently honoring [the Buddha] arises.
If they conceive a thought of "going" and take it to be going, then all doctrines concerning withered meditation and a parched nature arise.
If they conceive a thought of sitting or lying down and take it to be sitting or lying down, then whenever they encounter...
At every stupa and every temple, people claim that the Tathāgata sits or rests within them; thus, the notion of relying upon them arises once more.
Therefore, generally speaking, because they do not understand the meaning of what was taught, they perpetuate the delusions of later generations.
Not knowing the two characters "Tathāgata," one does not cling to forms or traces as the pivot of discourse. It is like a form following its shadow:

when the form ceases, the shadow vanishes of itself; when the form appears, the shadow manifests again. Form and shadow follow one another, appearing as if they were neither non-existent nor existent.
In truth, once this body is seen clearly in its coming and going, one will then believe clearly in this body;
seeing it as empty and void, one speaks the two lines: "It comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere."
Coming and going are not the point; the emphasis lies solely on the phrase "having nowhere from which to come. The subsequent phrase merely follows along with it.

Thus, the Tathāgata understands only the meaning of "coming" but does not understand the meaning of "going. If one views the character for "coming" (lai) as identical to the character for "going" (qu), then there would be a trace of coming.
To say "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) means to come according to one's true nature; thus, he comes together with birth itself.
This is the intended meaning. If there were such a thing as birth, yet it did not exist as something that comes along with its nature, what could be called "birth"?
When the Confucians speak of human birth, it is simply a gloss upon coming forth exactly according to one's nature.
Just by looking at the two characters "coming from" (zōnglái), one knows that that which comes and follows along is none other than what the Tathāgata (Rúlái) speaks of.
"Having nowhere from which [it comes]" does not mean that at the time of its arrival there is absolutely nothing from which it originates. This nature is most profoundly empty and numinous;
if one were to say from where it sets foot, a shadow would immediately follow. Therefore, it is said that it "has nowhere from which [it comes]."
Truly and truly, one sees the mind of perfect enlightenment; it is born simultaneously with birth and does not fall into any direction. Such is the subtle principle of this phrase.
For what reason is it said that one does not cling to extremes? Why, in the following phrase, is there the inclusion of the word "with"?
One can understand this by examining the single character "also" (yì). The Tathāgata merely speaks of the "Tathāgata"; he has never spoken of a "coming-from-suchness" (rúqù).
If one were to pit "coming" against "going," and employ the categories of past and future to frame arguments and impose retributions, it would utterly obscure the very face of the Tathāgata.
However, there is simply no place to which he goes. There is naturally an understanding: to speak of "coming" is to say he has "always come. To speak of...
That which departs is called "that which has departed. It returns to that very place from which it came.
That which comes does so in its entirety; that which departs does so without deficiency. Thus one knows that having departed, it returns again, remaining as it was before.
How can this not be called the Tathāgata? This is sufficient to convey the great significance of the Tathāgata.
Chapter Thirty: The Section on the Rational Characteristics.
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind the three-thousandfold world system into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of dust be great? Subhūti replied: It would be very much so, World-Honored One.
World-Honored One, why is this? If these multitudes of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called them "multitudes of atoms.
Why is that? The Buddha’s teaching that they are "multitudes of atoms" means they are not actually multitudes of atoms; it is merely designated as "multitudes of atoms.
World-Honored One, the so-called "trichiliocosm" spoken of by the Tathāgata is not actually a world; it is merely designated as a "world. Why is this?
For this reason, Subhūti, if a world were truly existent, it would be a "unified whole" (*piṇḍa-grāha*).
The Tathāgata says that what is called a "unified whole" is not a unified whole; it is merely designated as a "unified whole.
Subhūti, a unified whole is inexpressible; yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.

The Discourse on the Reality of the Son: Regarding the previous statement that the Tathāgata is without marks, it is because the nature of awakening eternally abides within the world, yet does not arise or perish together with the world. For this reason, he further uses a mote of dust as a metaphor for the world.
This is to clarify that there must not be even a single "mark of synthesis" (saṃghātalakṣaṇa).

Thus, the Tathāgata borrows the minuteness of a subtle particle (paramāṇu) to illustrate the vastness of a world-system, and then further shatters that vast world-system into the minuteness of subtle particles.

This is said to express, in extreme terms, the meaning of its being beyond description. Having reached the ultimate limit of the particle and spoken to the most minute point, it becomes visible to the eye.
It can be seen, yet the hand cannot grasp it; this is simply because the atoms are so numerous that they are difficult to hold.
Yunfeng said: "Speaking of atoms and speaking of worlds—this means that what is small cannot contain even a single mustard seed, while what is large can hide Mount Sumeru.
Yet the forms of both the small and the large are all ungraspable. Thus, he repeated this point over and over again.
Clarification: As for the statement that the trichiliocosm is shattered into minute particles (*paramāṇu*), this is an exaggeration to express how the great can be broken down into the small.
As for the statement that minute particles are equal to the trichiliocosm, this is an exaggeration to express how the small can contain the great.
In reality, because the Tathāgata could not exhaustively describe the profundities therein, he specifically used these [expressions].
This is clarified by means of an analogy. "Unity" (yīhé) refers to being unified such that it can no longer be divided.
Before there is the matter of union, the mind of union first arises. When the mind unites with the matter, they take form in relation to one another.

For example, when the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose have not yet given rise to a single thought, then color, sound, fragrance, and taste are entirely without form; yet once a thought arises and desire [is felt], [they appear].
When one looks, one accords with the characteristic of form. When a thought arises and one desires to hear, one accords with the characteristic of sound.
When a thought arises and one desires the mouth and nose to follow one’s intent, one accords with the characteristics of fragrance and flavor.
All these arise from a single thought, which then becomes entangled with these characteristics; this is precisely what is meant by "things interacting with things, drawing one along."
You have spoken.

You have truly spoken of this "single unified characteristic" (eka-lakṣaṇa). Should it be regarded as existent or non-existent? Can one discern its true message from within the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa)?
Yunfeng said: "Seek it further outside of dharmalakṣaṇa (phenomenal characteristics). Zizhen said:
"The arising of the 'unified totality' does not emerge from anything other than the person-self and the aggregates, nor from causes such as form and sound;
these are simply the Tathāgata. Once the marks of defilement are seen as empty, one awakens to the persistence of the true nature, wherein there is no attachment whatsoever. Within this:
Since there is no seeking of union from the outset, how could there ever be a single characteristic of union?
While the word "union" is easy to understand, the "single characteristic of union" is difficult to comprehend. To speak of "a single union" is like glue or lacquer adhering to an object:
initially they are not joined, yet as soon as they meet, they become so firmly fixed that they cannot be separated. This is why the characteristic of union is so prone to grasping and attachment.
The first [point] refers to speaking from the perspective of the initial thought-moment. As soon as that initial thought arises, one immediately falls into total delusion;

for this reason, such a person is called an "ordinary being" (*pṛthagjana*). The Tathāgata is without marks and not empty; how could there be any "unified mark" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) by which he might be named?
Chapter Thirty-one: On the Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, what do you think, Subhūti?
Would such a person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One, such a person would not. Subhūti, this person...

One understands the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this? World-Honored One, that which is called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span is itself not a view of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span;

it is merely designated as the "view of a self," the "view of a person," the "view of a sentient being," and the "view of a life-span. Subhūti, one who gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
In all dharmas, one should know them thus, see them thus, and resolve with faith thus, so that the mark of dharmas does not arise.
Subhūti, as for what is called the "mark of dharmas," the Tathāgata says it is not a mark of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "mark of dharmas."
The Discourse on the Reality of the Son: The Tathāgata further said, "I now explain the meaning of this sutra:

in reality, there is nothing whatsoever that possesses the four marks such that it could be described or perceived. If one first maintains within the mind the view that 'there is not one' of the four marks,"
These are the four marks. Yet there remains a persistent desire [to negate them]. Because they are said to be non-existent, many later people fail to understand the meaning of what was taught.
They think that since the four marks existed in the past but do not exist now, they must have been non-existent from the very beginning.
If they were non-existent from the start, what would constitute the four marks? Therefore, regarding their discourse on the self, persons, and sentient beings...
"O Āyuṣmat, that which is called a 'life-span' does not possess such characteristics; for when the Dharma is taught, there is nothing that can be pointed out—it is merely an empty name.
Within ultimate perfect awakening, how could there be the names of the four marks? Therefore, it is further said:
if one is able to realize this bodhicitta, one must certainly perceive with such a mind and recognize with such a mind."
When one explains the mind in this way, then wherever it may be, it is the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

How, then, could there be any characteristic of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) that can arise? This is because the characteristic of dharmas is merely the path for entering the gate, not the place of ultimate realization.
Therefore, it is used as a means of guidance, but one cannot realize the mind through it; hence, it is said: [The passage continues: "That which is spoken of..."
When one speaks of "characteristics of phenomena" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), what characteristic of phenomena could possibly remain?
It is merely a hollow name. Yunfeng said: Previously, it was stated that there are four characteristics—self, person, sentient being, and life-span.

Here, however, it is said that the term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) has a distinct meaning. To speak of "characteristics" implies that some characteristic still persists; to speak of "view," however, means that even the view of non-characteristic is absent.

Seeing and non-seeing pertain to the eyes; it is direct seeing that pertains to the mind. When the mind possesses this seeing, then even though the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) do not exist, one nonetheless clings to their existence.

Fearing that future generations might mistakenly believe the Tathāgata’s teaching because there are these four marks, and wishing to compel them to return to non-existence, he further clarified his statement, saying this for the following reason:
Within perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) are fundamentally non-existent; therefore, it is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and not a state of having marks.
Since one cannot forcibly compel something to return to non-existence, the word "see" (*dṛṣṭi*) is specifically mentioned. Furthermore, this is a deeper level than what was previously explained.
These three "Thusnesses" (*tathatā*) all refer to the bodhicitta. These three phrases correspond to the initial question regarding how one should abide.
In sum, having attained such knowledge, such vision, and such understanding, one should abide accordingly.
One does not give rise to the marks of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This corresponds to the initial question regarding how to subdue the mind;

for when one reaches the state where the marks of dharmas do not arise, there is no further arising or ceasing, and thus one should subdue the mind in this manner. This section has already reached its conclusion.
This concludes the essential meaning of the phrase "should have no abiding. One must not regard the three instances of the word "thus" (*iti*) as mere literal characters;
rather, they serve as connective terms that lead directly to the subsequent "suchness, immovable," and ultimately conclude with the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*).
The words "knowing," "seeing," and "faithful understanding" all serve to summarize the entire sutra. This is permitted [by the text].
There are many *huatou* (critical phrases). Furthermore, each character possesses discernment. For the wisdom of ordinary people arises from knowing;
if one does not know, there is nothing seen. It is only when the mind has something known that insight (*dṛṣṭi*) first emerges.
Once there is insight, one is then able to have faith and understanding. This refers to the four preceding fruits [of the śrāvaka] and up to the Bodhisattva Subhūti.
Ānanda, among all devas, humans, asuras, and sentient beings, there is no distinction of high or low;
it is only by means of this that one can realize prajñā. Those who recite, read, explain, or comment upon it must fix their eyes upon this point.
Chapter Thirty-Two: The Non-Reality of Manifested Transformations.

Subhūti, if someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift, and if there were a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta and upholds this sutra—even [for a brief moment]...
To receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain even four lines of verse from this sutra for others brings forth merit far superior to that.
How does one explain it for others? Without grasping at signs, remaining as suchness, immovable. Why is this so?
"All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them.

This was truly spoken by the Son [the Buddha]. Because the preceding section has already made it perfectly clear through the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), the final chapter merely employs the gift of giving as a pretext to bring forth the non-grasping of signs, thereby verifying the meaning of suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, it says: "If a person..."
If one were to take the seven treasures of immeasurable and innumerable worlds and give them as alms, this would be greater and more abundant than the sands of the Ganges;

yet it would still not equal the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining the meaning of this sutra and its four-line verse for others. This is because the merit of such giving is far superior.
Generosity still possesses marks; this, however, is markless.
Yunfeng said: "The reason for mentioning here only 'expounding it for others' is precisely because of the merit of saving sentient beings."
It is even more difficult than explaining for oneself. Therefore, while the *Yì* explains the meaning of characters, the *Zhuàn* elaborates upon their significance;

the former provides explanations based solely on the general purport, whereas the latter elaborates upon both the characters and the phrases themselves. Thus, the term "elaboration" (*zhuàn*) should be understood as "expanding the meaning" (*yǎn yì*).
This ensures that all people of future generations throughout the world will have no one who does not engage in such inference.
I have sought out the extensive commentaries, yet not a single word or phrase contains even the slightest ambiguity.
Your true teaching—how you expound it for the sake of others—is simply this:
because there is no mark of self or other (pudgala-ātman). Therefore, all marks whatsoever are unworthy of being grasped; and as for his mind, he acts accordingly.
In response: although one may be amidst a time of turbulent movement, within this state there is nonetheless suchness, unmoving.
Yunfeng’s commentary on the phrase "suchness, unmoving" states: the upper character "ru" (如) is empty; the lower character "ru" is real.
"Suchness" (ruru) means being exactly as it is. These two phrases correspond to the Confucian expressions "brightly clear" (mingming) and "serenely settled" (annan).

It is the same. Generally, the minds of ordinary people are characterized by much "not-as-it-should-be" (不如). Precisely because of this state of not being as it should be, the six sense objects and four marks cause turmoil;

amidst this, movement follows upon movement without end. When one reaches the stage of the sages and saints, whose enlightened nature is fully perfected, everything is "as-it-should-be" (如), and there is nothing that is not as it should be.
Because even slight obstructions have been removed, they are able to recognize the clear path of awakening.
It is exactly as it is. As for "suchness" (*tathatā*): by virtue of the single character "as" (*ru*), there is nothing that can be added or subtracted.
To subtract from it would mean it is not suchness; to add to it is likewise impossible.

Because it is suchness, the term "such-suchness" (*ruru*) is repeated to show that within it there is no room for even a single thing, yet it is limpid and profound—even when entering into the midst of turmoil.
Though external phenomena may stir, the center remains unmoved; all dharmas thus dissolve back into this.
This is the true countenance of the Tathāgata. The following four lines merely describe a single aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
the full purport has already been gathered within this sentence.
The Discourse on the Reality of the Son: Why is it that one does not grasp at appearances? It is because where there are appearances, there is conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
Where there is conditioned activity, one becomes attached to phenomena (*dharma*), and thus cannot remain in the state of suchness (*tathatā*) without movement.
This is precisely because all conditioned phenomena are devoid of anything to be grasped; they are like a dream upon waking, wherein the dream-scene becomes an illusion.
Like an illusion within existence, yet neither form nor sound can be grasped; like a bubble upon water, which ceases to exist as soon as it vanishes;
like a shadow following the body, which disappears the moment the body stops; and like the morning dew evaporating in the sun.
The light of an electric fire is extinguished; these six [elements] are all formless in an instant. How could there be any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) to be grasped?
Therefore, it is said that one should contemplate conditioned phenomena in this manner through these six points.
Yunfeng said: "To say that such contemplation cannot be fixed upon as 'six'—the number six is merely a metaphorical expression;
how can it be grasped as something definitive? The general meaning is still that which was taught by the Buddha. If a person can recognize the principle of true emptiness and formlessness,"
Thus, it is so in every instance. How could there be anything that cannot be contemplated? This phrase opens up a single teaching:
one may then fully integrate the two polarities and the four images into the Great Ultimate (*tàijí*), and completely empty the six sense objects and the four marks within Suchness (*rúru*).
One who contemplates can penetrate from beginning to end, becoming brilliantly illuminated within this state of "thusness" (*rúshì*).
...it is so. This is precisely how the meaning of the Tathāgata’s sutra arises and ceases together with heaven and earth.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās]...
The upāsikā, all the worldlings, devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

The Discourse on the True Son: At that time, when the Tathāgata had finished preaching this sutra, those who heard it—such as Subhūti, who was the elder among the disciples, as well as the bhikṣus known by the name of the Saṃgha—[were present].
Among the assembly of nuns known as bhikṣuṇīs, among the sons of good family known as upāsakas,
among the daughters of good family known as upāsikās, and even among the devas, humans, and kingly ghosts known as asuras—
there was not one who did not hear the meaning of the sūtra preached by the Tathāgata, thereby giving rise to a heart of joy and receiving, upholding, and practicing it with faith.
Yunfeng said: "To hear it and yet not believe it is to hear it in vain. To believe it and yet not practice it is to rejoice in vain.

He concludes the chapter with these four words so that those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this sutra for others may have both a beginning and an end, ensuring they do not fall into negligence or indolence. Thus it is said:
The teaching of the [Buddha] has been constantly practiced throughout heaven and earth.

Yet, this sutra shall fortunately remain; and among those sentient beings, for those who repent and reform themselves, the Tathāgata will, by means of Bodhi...
He focused his mind and led them to ascend to the other shore. One can see that when the Tathāgata spoke of the final age, he himself harbored the intention of protecting the Dharma.

It was at this time that the śramaṇas reached their greatest prosperity, yet it was also at this time they reached their greatest decline. Thus, the Wei ruler constructed a stūpa of such great height...
